questions.q: Graphene's electrons move very fast. Why can it not make a good transistor on its own?
options: It has no band gap, so it cannot be switched fully off
It is too fragile to survive being patterned into a transistor
At one atom thick, the gate's field passes straight through it
Its electrons move too fast for the gate to control them
questions.explain: Graphene's conduction and valence bands touch, so it has no band gap: there is no energy range without states, and a graphene transistor cannot be switched fully off.

questions.q: The picture shows a sheet of graphene being rolled up. Why is the resulting nanotube an ideal channel to wrap a gate around?
questions.alt: Three panels of carbon atoms: a flat honeycomb sheet, the sheet partly rolled, and a seamless tube
options: It has no edges or dangling bonds, and is only 1–2 nm across
It is hollow, so the gate can be placed inside it as well as outside
It is always metallic, so it conducts without any doping
Its surface is covered in dangling bonds that hold the gate oxide in place
questions.explain: A nanotube is a graphene sheet rolled into a seamless cylinder 1–2 nm across. It has no edges and no dangling bonds, and the gate can be wrapped all round it.

questions.q: What decides whether a carbon nanotube is a metal or a semiconductor?
options: The angle at which the sheet is rolled; about one tube in three is a metal
The length of the tube; tubes longer than 1 µm are metals
The gas used to grow it; tubes grown from methane are semiconductors
Its diameter alone: thin tubes are semiconductors and wide tubes are metals
questions.explain: The rolling angle decides the electrical type, and about one tube in three is metallic. Growth produces a mixture, which is the main manufacturing headache.

questions.q: The graph shows the band gap of semiconducting nanotubes against their diameter. Roughly what is the gap of a 1.5 nm tube?
questions.alt: Band gap against tube diameter from 0.6 to 3 nm: a falling curve, with silicon's 1.12 eV marked as a dashed line and the 1.2–1.8 nm range shaded as useful for transistors
options: About 0.5 eV, roughly half of silicon's
About 1.1 eV, the same as silicon's
About 2 eV, nearly twice silicon's
About 0.25 eV, a quarter of silicon's
questions.explain: The gap is about 0.8 eV divided by the diameter in nm: about 0.5 eV for a 1.5 nm tube, half of silicon's. Wider tubes leak more; thinner ones are hard to contact, so transistors use 1.2–1.8 nm tubes.

questions.q: In a nanotube transistor with metal contacts, how does a high gate voltage switch the current on?
options: It bends the bands down so the barrier at the contact becomes thin, and electrons tunnel through it
It heats the contact so that electrons gain enough energy to jump over the barrier
It lowers a hill in the middle of the channel, as in a MOSFET
It pulls extra electrons out of the gate and into the tube
questions.explain: Where metal meets tube there is a barrier. With the gate low it is thick and electrons are stopped; with the gate high the bands bend down, the barrier becomes thin, and electrons tunnel through.

questions.q: True or false: with doped tube ends instead of metal contacts, the gate switches the nanotube transistor by thinning a barrier at the contacts.
options: True
False
questions.explain: False. With doped ends there is no contact barrier to thin. The gate raises or lowers a hill in the channel and electrons flow over it, as in a MOSFET: one carrier type and a swing close to 60 mV per decade.

questions.q: The graph shows the current of a nanotube transistor with metal contacts against gate voltage. Why is the curve V-shaped?
questions.alt: Drain current per tube on a log scale against gate voltage from −0.8 to 1.2 V for three tube diameters: each curve has a sharp minimum near 0.2 V and rises on both sides
options: A high gate voltage lets electrons in, and a low gate voltage lets holes in
The tube heats up at both ends of the sweep, and heat raises the current
The gate oxide leaks at both high and low gate voltages
Wider tubes leak at both ends of the sweep, while narrow tubes do not
questions.explain: With metal contacts, a high gate voltage thins the barrier for electrons and a low gate voltage thins it for holes, so the current rises at both ends: a V. Doped contacts allow one carrier only, which makes the better transistor.

questions.q: Electrons cross a nanotube shorter than about 1 µm without colliding. What is this called?
options: Ballistic transport
Thermionic emission
Diffusion
Avalanche breakdown
questions.explain: Ballistic transport: with no collisions, the current is limited only by the number of lanes (four in a nanotube), and the minimum resistance, about 6.45 kΩ, is paid at the contacts.

questions.q: Why do large nanotube circuits need tubes that are better than 99.9999% semiconducting?
options: A metallic tube cannot be switched off, so its transistor leaks
Metallic tubes switch on at a different gate voltage, which upsets the timing
Metallic tubes are much wider, so they push the other tubes out of line
Metallic tubes have a high contact resistance, which slows the whole circuit
questions.explain: A metallic tube has no gap, so the gate cannot switch it off: it keeps conducting and the transistor leaks. With billions of transistors, even one metallic tube in a million matters.

questions.q: Nanotubes are not doped like silicon. How are p-type and n-type nanotube transistors usually made?
options: By the contact metal: palladium gives p-type, scandium gives n-type
By how the tube is rolled: zigzag tubes p-type, armchair tubes n-type
By the gate oxide: SiO₂ gives p-type and HfO₂ gives n-type
By the growth temperature: hot-grown p-type, cold-grown n-type
questions.explain: Choosing the metal chooses n or p. Palladium lines up with the valence band, so holes enter easily: p-type. Scandium lines up with the conduction band: n-type.
